focus: Focus on the results at 2 and 4 weeks.
modelNote:
Create a clean, professional portrait infographic for a university student summarising the research paper “Decreasing students’ stress through time management training: an intervention study” by Alexander Häfner, Armin Stock & Verena Oberst, Eur J Psychol Educ (2015) 30:81–94. Focus mainly on the results at 2 and 4 weeks.

STRICT CONTENT RULES: Use only the information below. Do not add any outside facts, examples, numbers, or interpretations. Preserve hedges and strength of claim. Spell all words correctly. Every number displayed must exactly match the paper.

STYLE: Tall portrait layout, university-friendly, readable, clean hierarchy. Use icons, simple line charts or bar charts, and short text blocks. White background with muted blue/teal and orange accents. Large title at top. Prefer fewer, larger text blocks. Avoid tiny dense tables.

TITLE:
“Time Management Training: Results After 2 and 4 Weeks”
SUBTITLE:
“Häfner, Stock & Oberst (2015) — undergraduate students at a medium-sized German university”

SECTION 1: STUDY SNAPSHOT (small top panel with icons)
- “Main analysis: n = 23 undergraduate students”
- “Training: 4 h time management intervention”
- “Measurements: before training, 2 weeks after, 4 weeks after”
- “Design: non-equivalent dependent variable design”
Use a simple timeline: Before training → 2 weeks → 4 weeks.

SECTION 2: WHAT THE TRAINING COVERED (compact row of 5 icons)
Label: “Training strategies”
Icons/text:
1. Prioritizing
2. Goal setting
3. Strategy development
4. Daily planning
5. Monitoring
Keep this secondary; the infographic’s focus is results.

SECTION 3: MAIN RESULTS BY TIME POINT (central visual focus)
Use two side-by-side panels or stacked cards labelled “2 weeks after training” and “4 weeks after training”.

2 WEEKS CARD:
- Stress (tension): “Significantly less than before training”
- show mean scores as a simple before/after mini chart:
  Before: M = 3.30, SD = 0.57
  2 weeks: M = 2.96, SD = 0.71
- statistics: “F(1, 22) = 8.22, partial η² = 0.27, p < 0.01”
- Perceived control of time: “Tendency in expected direction; not significant”
- mini chart:
  Before: M = 2.75, SD = 0.57
  2 weeks: M = 2.89, SD = 0.51
- statistics: “F(1, 22) = 3.38, partial η² = 0.13, p = 0.08”
- Overall time effect: “F(2, 21) = 4.09, partial η² = 0.28, p = 0.03”

4 WEEKS CARD:
- Stress (tension): “Significantly less than before training”
- mini chart:
  Before: M = 3.30, SD = 0.57
  4 weeks: M = 3.03, SD = 0.72
- statistics: “F(1, 22) = 5.75, partial η² = 0.21, p = 0.03”
- Perceived control of time: “Significantly higher than before training”
- mini chart:
  Before: M = 2.75, SD = 0.57
  4 weeks: M = 3.05, SD = 0.52
- statistics: “F(1, 22) = 11.62, partial η² = 0.35, p < 0.01”
- Overall time effect: “F(2, 21) = 6.01, partial η² = 0.36, p < 0.01”

SECTION 4: CONTROL VARIABLE — DEMANDS (smaller but clear)
Heading: “Demands did not significantly change”
Important wording: “Demands means perceived, self-reported demands.”
Show a simple 3-point line or dot chart with exact means:
Before: M = 3.59, SD = 0.69
2 weeks: M = 3.35, SD = 0.69
4 weeks: M = 3.46, SD = 0.61
Add exact tests:
- “Before vs. 2 weeks: t(22) = 1.68, p = 0.107”
- “Before vs. 4 weeks: t(22) = 1.19, p = 0.251”

SECTION 5: TRANSFER OF STRATEGIES (small panel)
Heading: “Did students use the strategies?”
Text:
- “Time management behaviour increased significantly from before training to 4 weeks after training.”
- “Before: M = 3.01, SD = 0.55”
- “2 weeks: M = 3.19, SD = 0.48 — nearly significant increase from before training: t(22) = 1.62, p = 0.060 (one-tailed), ε′ = 0.48”
- “4 weeks: M = 3.31, SD = 0.55 — significant increase from before training: t(22) = 2.67, p < 0.01 (one-tailed), ε′ = 0.79”

SECTION 6: INTERPRETATION + LIMITATION (bottom takeaway strip)
Heading: “Takeaway”
Text:
“After the 4 h training, students reported less perceived stress at 2 and 4 weeks, and higher perceived control of time at 4 weeks. Demands did not significantly change. The authors conclude that time management training might be beneficial for undergraduate students’ well-being.”
Limitation box:
“Main limitation: small sample. The authors describe the study as preliminary and say more intervention studies with larger samples are necessary.”

VISUAL NOTES:
- Use downward arrow for stress/tension, upward arrow for perceived control of time, neutral icon for demands.
- Avoid saying “proved” or “caused” in a strong unqualified way. If using cause language, attribute to authors: “authors conclude”.
- Do NOT include percentages from cited studies or external background.
- Do NOT calculate differences or percentages.
- Make charts readable, with exact means printed next to markers/bars.
- Ensure “perceived stress” is labelled as “Stress (tension)” wherever the measured outcome appears.
